item.title: Verifying a download
item.description:
Each release of authnd, authn-bridge, authn-revokd and sshcert publishes six static binaries (CGO_ENABLED=0: linux, darwin and windows, on amd64 and arm64), a SHA256SUMS file, and a build-provenance attestation for every binary. The examples below use authn-bridge v0.20.1; the other programs work the same way with their own repository and name.

gh release download v0.20.1 --repo go-authn/bridge

1. The checksum 

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # macOS: shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
authn-bridge-darwin-amd64: OK
authn-bridge-darwin-arm64: OK
authn-bridge-linux-amd64: OK
authn-bridge-linux-arm64: OK
authn-bridge-windows-amd64.exe: OK
authn-bridge-windows-arm64.exe: OK

This proves the file is the one the release lists, and nothing more: whoever could replace a binary on the release page could replace SHA256SUMS beside it.

2. The provenance 

gh attestation verify authn-bridge-linux-amd64 --repo go-authn/bridge
echo $?

The attestation is signed by GitHub for the workflow run that built the file, so it names the repository and the workflow, not a key somebody holds.

Read the exit status, not the output. Without a terminal, some versions of gh print nothing at all when the verification succeeds: measured with gh 2.65.0 on authnd, a genuine binary gave exit status 0 and an empty output. A binary with one byte appended gave exit status 1 and Error: failed to fetch attestations from go-authn/authnd: HTTP 404: Not Found, because no attestation exists for its digest. Silence is not the failure; a non-zero status is.

3. What the binary says about itself 

go version -m authn-bridge-linux-amd64
 path github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge
mod github.com/go-authn/bridge v0.20.1
build -trimpath=true
build CGO_ENABLED=0
build vcs.revision=d30d3b52b644c7db74c431c2a07b8d1aaeb1c0ff
build vcs.modified=false

(lines shortened to the ones that matter). The mod line must be the tag exactly, and vcs.modified must be false: a build from a tree with uncommitted changes says true, and its version reads v0.20.1+dirty. The release workflow refuses to publish unless every one of the six binaries passes both checks, and unless the program prints the tag as the last word of its version line:

$ authnd --version
authnd version v0.10.1
$ authn-bridge --version
authn-bridge version v0.20.1
$ authn-revokd -version
authn-revokd v0.6.2

authnd and authn-bridge take --version; authn-revokd takes -version, Go’s standard flag syntax. From v0.6.1 it prints on standard output, like the other two, so v=$(authn-revokd -version) captures it.

Which releases have binaries

Binaries, sums and attestations are published from authnd v0.9.2, authn-bridge v0.19.3, authn-revokd v0.5.0 and sshcert v0.1.2. The first release of each built its binaries inside the checkout and reported +dirty; that was fixed in the next one, and the per-binary check came after that. Earlier tags are source-only: build them with go install …@<tag>, which records the tag in the build information that go version -m reads. What the program prints is not always that: sshcert-authorize printed dev for a go install build until v0.1.5, and revokd has no -version before v0.5.0.

item.title: Status
item.description:
These pages are documentation version 0.1, and describe:

program release module
authnd v0.10.1 github.com/go-authn/authnd
authn-bridge v0.20.1 github.com/go-authn/bridge
authn-revokd v0.6.2 github.com/go-authn/revocation
sshcert-authorize v0.1.5 github.com/go-authn/sshcert

The libraries’ versions are on their own page. A new minor version of any program above is a new documentation version, so the pages a reader finds under /docs/0.1/ keep describing what they installed.

What each release added

Each line is the change a release was cut for. Releases that only updated dependencies are left out.

authnd

v0.1.0 an LDAP server for people who are somewhere else: a file, a SQL database, another directory
v0.2.0 a second factor, over a protocol with one field
v0.5.0 password changes that touch exactly one identity; a reload with no race; the KDC sees changes
v0.6.0 the security fixes of oidc, directory, ldap, totp and mfa
v0.7.0 the old password is required to change one; secrets are compared as fixed-length digests
v0.8.2 a code counts only behind the right password; a reader is keyed by its configured DN
v0.9.0 built and tested with Go 1.27.1, pinned rather than stable
v0.9.2 release binaries, SHA256SUMS and build provenance on every tag
v0.9.3 binaries built outside the checkout; each must report the tag exactly
v0.9.4 a SIGHUP no longer ends authnd: it is logged, and nothing is reloaded
v0.9.5 the release checks every binary’s build information, not one
v0.9.6 check says why each person cannot be issued a ticket
v0.10.0 check opens the certificate and the keytab, as the server does; it names who cannot bind with a password, and who a token still admits; the listening line comes after the realm opens
v0.10.1 go-authn/kdc v0.4.2: a till of 19700101000000Z gets the longest ticket, not one expired in 1970

authn-bridge

v0.1.0 an OpenID Connect provider in front of a SAML federation
v0.2.0 the device grant, SSH certificates, application passwords, OpenPubkey
v0.3.0 an admin API (bridge.admin.v1), and /healthz, /readyz, /metrics
v0.4.0 ES256 access tokens
v0.5.0 TLS through go-authn/servercert, shared with go-fileshare
v0.6.0 certificates that can be revoked: an SSH KRL, and X.509 for NFS with a CRL
v0.7.0 state that survives a restart: refresh tokens and honoured access tokens
v0.8.0 a Shared Signals transmitter: CAEP session-revoked
v0.9.0 the fixes of an adversarial review of v0.8.1
v0.10.0 revocation lists to be checked anywhere: a signed KRL, an expiry, an ETag of the content
v0.10.2 a CRL number for every issue; never an issue dated before the last
v0.11.0 groups held to their identity provider; disabling by identity; a bridge-only audience
v0.12.0 a login in progress lives in its sealed cookie, not in memory
v0.13.0 a confidential client may protect its code with the nonce (RFC 9700 2.1.1)
v0.16.0 max_age asks for a new authentication only when the last is too old
v0.16.3 a second review: every spelling revoked, disabling by sub, no replay across restarts
v0.17.0 WireGuard keys, registered by people and listed for a gateway
v0.18.0 an ID token without the person’s claims; go-authn/saml v0.4.0
v0.19.0 the EuroHPC SSH CA profile, opt-in per client
v0.19.3 release binaries, SHA256SUMS and build provenance on every tag
v0.20.0 the command is authn-bridge; a hardened systemd unit and an install guide
v0.20.1 comments and a refusal message that were no longer true; the README lists everything RevokePerson revokes

authn-revokd

v0.1.0 signed, expiring revocation lists: the protocol, the library, and revokd (agent and mirror)
v0.2.0 the fixes of an adversarial review
v0.2.1 each CA’s list merged with its own key revocations; a CRL’s signature checked before it is parsed
v0.3.0 key revocations scoped; failing closed per CA; the state directory’s owner checked
v0.5.0 release binaries, SHA256SUMS and build provenance on every tag
v0.6.0 the command is authn-revokd; systemd units and an install guide; SIGHUP syncs at once
v0.6.1 -version prints on standard output
v0.6.2 -once tells a failed fetch apart from a lapsed list; a list signed by another key is no longer called a race; -help exits 0

sshcert

v0.1.0 the domain-grant extension, and a fail-closed sshcert-authorize
v0.1.2 release binaries, SHA256SUMS and build provenance on every tag
v0.1.4 the release checks every binary’s build information
v0.1.5 -version prints the module version of a go install build, not dev

Not implemented yet

  • Writes through LDAP, beyond a person changing their own password. authnd answers a modify of one’s own userPassword and the RFC 3062 password modify operation (what ldappasswd sends), both only with the current password, and nothing else: add, delete and modifyDN exist in go-authn/ldap and are deliberately not wired (server.go). The library carries a modify as an ordered list (RFC 4511 4.6) and answers the read entry controls (RFC 4527), so the shape is there; what is missing is the policy of who may write what.
  • A second factor inside Kerberos: OTP pre-authentication (RFC 6560) in FAST (RFC 6113). Until it exists, a kerberos block and an mfa block cannot both be configured.
  • RC4-HMAC: the realm issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 only, so a person known only by an NT hash cannot be issued a ticket. This is a choice (RC4 is deprecated by RFC 8429), not a gap waiting to be filled.
